lines.text: Monday, Ben's agent spends two hours on a flaky build, and finally cracks it. Tuesday, Ada's agent hits the same build, and starts from zero.
The fix lived in one chat, on one laptop. Multiply that by every teammate and every lesson, and hours go to rediscovering what somebody already knows.
Agent R Q Teams fixes that. You share workspaces with your teammates, and you choose how much of each one: tasks, memory, skills, and Panno docs.
First, getting everyone on board. Usually that means a shared login, or an admin setting things up for days.
Here, you create a team in one step. Type a name, like Platform, and you are its first member.
Then invite a teammate by email address. Agent R Q gives you a link to send, in chat or by email.
Ben opens the link and joins. He keeps his own account, his own agents, and his own workspaces. No shared password anywhere.
Now the team has two members. There are no owners or admins: any member can invite someone, or remove them.
And the activity log names who did what, so every change has a name next to it.
Next, standup. What are Ben's agents doing right now? Normally everyone asks, and everyone scrolls back through old chats.
Ada opens the team settings, and switches on one workspace, the storefront. Sharing is decided per workspace, never for the whole account.
Ben shares his storefront too. Same name, so the two become one team workspace. There is nothing to configure, and each of them still runs their own agents.
Now both see every storefront task live, with the owner's name on each one. Ada sees Ben is already fixing the signup email, so she picks something else.
Filter by member to see only Ben's work, or open the team board.
Team analytics count what got done this week, across everyone.
It is all read-only. Ada cannot reply to Ben's agent, or approve anything for him. But if a task is useful, she can clone it into her own workspace, run by her own agent.
Now, the Monday fix. Agents learn something every day, and the lesson stays in one session.
With memory shared, each agent's memory lists every teammate's memory next to its own.
So on Monday, Ben's agent saves what it learned as a short note: clear the build cache, then run the end-to-end tests.
On Tuesday, Ada's agent loads its memory, finds Ben's note, and reads it first. It clears the cache, the build goes green, and two hours become two minutes.
An agent only ever writes to its own memory. Teammates can read Ben's note, but nobody can overwrite it.
Then the playbooks. Ada, Ben and Chen each keep a release skill, and every copy has quietly drifted.
In a team workspace, the team owns its skills. Every member's agent can use them and improve them, and each workspace opts in.
Ben's agent adds the missing tagging step. One edit, in one place. The file goes from version one to version two, so nothing is overwritten by accident.
On the next release, Ada's agent loads the skill and follows every step, including the one it never knew.
And plans. Ada wrote the launch plan, and the team needs it. But her other drafts are not ready for anyone.
So she opens the plan on her Panno, and the share switch sits right on the doc. She shares it with Platform. Only that doc moves.
Ben reads it on the team Panno. He cannot edit it, so nobody changes the plan behind Ada's back.
His agent can read it too, and picks up the checklist.
Ada can unshare it whenever she likes, and the team loses access at once.
Then Chen joins on Monday, and Chen's agent knows nothing about the project.
Chen accepts the invite, and shares a storefront workspace. It joins the team workspace on its own.
On the first task, Chen's agent loads the team's memory and the release skill, and gets it right the first time. No weeks of questions in chat.
And you stay in control. Nothing is shared just because you joined. Tasks, memory and skills each have their own switch, per workspace.
Turn one off, and the team stops seeing it right away. Leave the team, and every share stops with you.
Agents obey the same switches. A teammate's agent reads only what you chose to share.
Solve it once, and the whole team keeps it. Live tasks, shared memory, one playbook, and the docs you choose.
What has one of your agents learned that the rest of your team still does not know? Tell us in the comments, and try Teams at Agent R Q dot com.
